definition: A second, earlier preparatory motion that anticipates the anticipation itself — the body winds up for its own wind-up — rather than a single preparatory phase before the main action.
purpose: Read an especially forceful or complex action (a baseball-pitcher-style throw, a haymaker) as more powerful than a single-level anticipation can communicate, by giving the audience two beats of load-up instead of one.
visible_effect: Two (or more) distinct preparatory sub-phases before the main action, often in different or opposing directions — e.g. a step forward, then a wind-up, then the arm thrown back, then the punch.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Reads as a bigger, more consequential action than the same motion with one anticipation phase; costs proportionally more time, so it trades responsiveness for perceived weight even more than ordinary anticipation does.
physical_interpretation: Loading energy in stages, the way a pitcher's full-body windup loads more energy than a wrist flick — an extension of anticipation's own spring analogy to multiple linked springs.
use_cases: a signature or "finisher" attack meant to read as the most powerful action in its moveset
a boss telegraph that must be unmistakable even from a distance
a comedic take where a character absurdly over-prepares for a small action
non_use_cases: ordinary or frequent actions, where the extra duration compounds anticipation's own responsiveness cost past what a game can afford
any action whose single-level anticipation is already at the limit the design permits
a surprise or reflex reaction, where even one level of anticipation should stay minimal
interactions: Anticipation — this is a specialization of it, not a separate principle; both share the same readability-vs-responsiveness tradeoff (Part 26.2)
Timing — each added level multiplies the cost against the action's total duration, so this is timing's tradeoff compounded
Exaggeration — layering anticipation is itself a form of exaggerating the preparation phase specifically, restrained everywhere else

style_variations.anime: a natural fit — held multi-beat windups before a signature attack are a genre convention
style_variations.realistic: rare — most real preparatory motion is a single continuous load, not distinct beats
style_variations.game_combat: reserved for the smallest number of highest-impact moves in a kit, given the responsiveness cost

cadence_representation: Not represented. `ai/cal.js PHASE_NAMES` and `ai/plan.js segmentPhases` locate at most one `anticipation` phase per action from key/marker evidence — nothing in this build distinguishes a second, earlier sub-phase from the first, so a layered wind-up would currently segment as a single (longer, oddly-shaped) anticipation phase rather than two.
control_surface: None directly. `anticipation_depth` scales whatever single phase `segmentPhases` finds; there is no way to address an inner sub-phase separately.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js` measures onset/peak per joint, which could in principle locate a direction reversal WITHIN an already-segmented anticipation phase (a second local extremum before the main action's onset) — but no code in this build runs that search; it is a real, not merely theoretical, extension of an existing measurement.
generation_or_modification_methods: None. Inserting a second preparatory phase requires adding keys, which `ai/plan.js` strategies do not do (Phase 3's planner may not add or remove a key, per CLAUDE.md).
failure_modes: layering anticipation on an action too minor to earn the extra time, reading as sluggish rather than powerful
two anticipation phases that move in the same direction instead of a distinct second beat, which reads as one slow phase rather than two
applying it to a gameplay-critical action where the compounded responsiveness cost breaks the input feel
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure keyframe-timing structure, independent of the target engine.
performance_implications: None beyond any other keyframe edit — no simulation or particle cost.
examples: a baseball-pitcher-style throw: step forward, wind up, throw the other arm back, then punch (video 1 @ 3:50–4:11)
a boss slowly raising a weapon overhead, pausing, then raising it further before the strike
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/uDqjIdI4bF4 @ 3:47–4:13 — Alan Becker narrates and shows a punch with two nested wind-up phases, contrasted against the same punch with a single anticipation phase; experimental until validated
